prompt:
Write an explanation of about 1,200 words of how public-key cryptography lets two people who have never met agree on a secret over a line that others can listen to. The reader has school-level maths and no computing background.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists.

Write it in this voice: Calm, even register. Mostly medium-length, complete sentences, with length set by content rather than rhythm. No pattern of a short hook paid off by a longer sentence. Plain words over writerly ones, and lines allowed to sit flat. Numbers, names and concrete facts carry the point instead of abstractions. Em dashes, parentheticals, adverbs, doublets and parallelism kept rare. Descriptive writing states what a thing is and does, and any view is labelled as a view. British spelling.

text:
Two people who want to exchange private messages usually begin with a shared secret, such as a password or a code book. If they have never met, they have no such secret, and the only way to give one to the other is to send it along a line that anyone may be listening to. This looks impossible, because a person who hears every word of the conversation hears the secret as well. It can be done, though, and your phone does it with websites many times a day. The method was published in 1976 by Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman. It rests on a kind of arithmetic that is quick to do in one direction and slow to undo.

The arithmetic is the remainder left after a division. Imagine a clock with 23 hours on its face instead of 12. If it is 20 o'clock and you wait 5 hours, the clock shows 2, because 25 divided by 23 leaves a remainder of 2. Mathematicians call this working modulo 23. Every number is replaced by its remainder after dividing by 23, so every answer is a whole number from 0 to 22. Powers work in the same way. 5 to the power of 2 is 25, which shows as 2 on this clock. 5 to the power of 3 is 125, which is five lots of 23 plus 10, so it shows as 10.

If you keep going with powers of 5 on this clock, you get 5, 2, 10, 4, 20, 8, 17, 16, 11 and 9 for the first ten. The list jumps around with no pattern that helps you guess the next entry. Working forwards is simple: you pick a power and calculate the result. Working backwards is harder. If someone tells you the answer was 19 and asks which power of 5 produced it, the only general method is to try the powers one after another until 19 turns up. It turns up at the fifteenth. With a clock of 23 hours that takes a minute. The whole method depends on the clock being much larger, as we will see.

Now take two people, Alice and Bob, with Eve listening to everything they say. Alice and Bob agree out loud on two public numbers, which are 23 for the clock and 5 for the base. Eve hears these and it does not matter. Alice then chooses a private number, say 6, and tells no one. She works out 5 to the power of 6, which is 15,625, and finds its remainder after dividing by 23. That is 8, since 23 times 679 is 15,617. She sends 8 to Bob. Bob chooses his own private number, say 15, and works out 5 to the power of 15 on the same clock. That gives 19, and he sends 19 to Alice. Eve has now heard 23, 5, 8 and 19. She has not heard 6 or 15.

Next, Alice takes the 19 she received from Bob and raises it to the power of her private number, 6. She finds that 19 to the power of 6 is 47,045,881, and its remainder after dividing by 23 is 2. Bob takes the 8 he received from Alice and raises it to the power of his private number, 15, which gives 2 as well. They have the same number, and neither of them ever sent it. The reason is that Bob's 19 is 5 to the power of 15, so Alice has worked out 5 to the power of 15, raised to the power of 6. Bob's 8 is 5 to the power of 6, so he has worked out 5 to the power of 6, raised to the power of 15. Both come to 5 to the power of 90, because 15 times 6 and 6 times 15 are the same number. On this clock, 5 to the power of 90 shows as 2. That is their shared secret.

Eve's task is to find the same 2 with what she has heard. She knows that 5 to some power gave 8 and that 5 to another power gave 19. To get the secret she needs one of those powers, and she can only find it by trial. On a clock of 23 hours she would read it from the list above in a few seconds, so the numbers in this example would protect nothing. Real systems use a clock with a prime number of hours that is about 617 digits long, which is 2,048 binary digits as a computer counts them. The private numbers are of similar length. The number of possible powers is then about 10 followed by 616 zeros, and the observable universe is thought to hold about 10 followed by 80 zeros of atoms. Trying each power in turn is out of the question. Mathematicians have found methods that are faster than trial for some clocks, and the real systems choose their numbers to stay out of reach of those. Nobody has proved that no fast method exists, so the safety rests on decades of failed attempts to find one.

Alice's 8 and her private 6 are what give the field its name. The private number is her private key, and the number she sends is her public key. A public key can be printed in a directory or sent to a stranger, because knowing it does not let anyone work out the private key behind it. Anyone who holds Alice's public key can use it with a private number of their own to agree a secret with her. A second scheme, published in 1977 by Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman, uses a different one-way task. Multiplying two very large primes takes a computer a moment, while splitting their product back into those primes is out of reach. That scheme lets anyone lock a message using a public key so that only the owner of the matching private key can open it. It is also true that three British mathematicians at GCHQ, James Ellis, Clifford Cocks and Malcolm Williamson, reached these ideas in the early 1970s. Their work was classified and was not made public until 1997.

The shared secret is not used to write messages directly. Once both sides hold the same number, they use it as the key for an ordinary cipher such as AES, which scrambles data quickly and can only be reversed by someone holding that key. Public-key methods are slower, so they are used for the opening exchange and the cipher does the bulk of the work. Eve, who recorded the whole session, has a stream of scrambled data and no key.

The method has one weakness that the arithmetic cannot fix. Alice does not know that the number she received came from Bob. Suppose a fourth person, Mallory, can change what travels along the line. Mallory can run one exchange with Alice and another with Bob, and pass the messages between them while reading each one. Neither of them would notice. Browsers deal with this by checking certificates, which are statements that a particular public key belongs to a particular website. Each certificate is signed by an organisation that the browser already trusts. This is a matter of who you believe, and it depends on people and procedures as well as mathematics. Most current systems also use a variant built on the points of an elliptic curve instead of a clock, which gives the same protection with much shorter numbers. A large quantum computer, if one is built, would be able to undo the clock problem quickly, and work is under way on replacements.
